541.quote_or_event: “For the king, cleansing is justice; for the scholar, it is true meditation.”
541.explanation: Rejecting ritual purity, Guru Nanak says that what truly purifies each person is the duty of his station, and for a ruler that duty is justice.
541.tie_back: The Kural defines the right sceptre as justice done without favour after careful inquiry; Guru Nanak likewise makes justice the king's essential practice.
541.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1240, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
541._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on justice as the king's defining duty; the salok does not describe the Kural's procedure of impartial inquiry and consultation.

542.quote_or_event: “Leaving the water, the fish cannot live; the rainbird cannot live without the raindrops from the clouds.”
542.explanation: Guru Arjan uses the rainbird's total dependence on rain from the clouds as an image of the soul's dependence on God.
542.tie_back: The Kural says the people live looking to the sceptre as all living things look to the sky for rain; Guru Arjan uses the same picture of life hanging on rain from above, though for him the dependence is on God, not a king.
542.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 708, Raag Jaithsree (Jaithsree ki Vaar), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
542._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the rain-dependence image matches, but Gurbani applies it to devotion to God rather than to subjects and their ruler.

543.quote_or_event: In 1609 Guru Hargobind built the Akal Takht at Amritsar, a temple and assembly hall where both the spiritual and the temporal affairs of the Sikh community could be settled, and he bore two swords for his twin authority, temporal (miri) and spiritual (piri).
543.explanation: From Hargobind onward Sikh tradition joins temporal authority to the spiritual, with temporal power set to guard the community's faith.
543.tie_back: The Kural says the king's sceptre is the foundation that keeps the sages' scriptures and dharma standing; in Sikh tradition the seat of temporal authority stands to protect the life of the Guru's word.
543._accuracy_note: Good fit on temporal power sustaining religion, though in Sikhism miri is subordinate to and derived from piri, not the source of scripture as Parimelazhagar's Vedic reading implies.

544.quote_or_event: “Let no one chase after and attack anyone else. Let all abide in peace, under this Benevolent Rule.”
544.explanation: Guru Arjan proclaims halemi raj, a gentle and benevolent rule under the merciful Lord's command, in which no one harms another and all live at ease.
544.tie_back: The Kural says the world clings to the feet of the king who rules embracing his people; Guru Arjan's benevolent rule, where all abide in peace, is the Sikh picture of such rule.
544.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 74, Siree Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
544._accuracy_note: Reasonable: the ideal of gentle rule matches, but many commentators read halemi raj as the inner reign of humility under God rather than an earthly kingdom.

545.quote_or_event: “The rain has fallen; I have found the Transcendent Lord God.”
545.explanation: Guru Arjan uses the coming of the rain as an image of grace and fulfilment.
545.tie_back: The Kural says seasonal rain and rich harvests belong together in the land of a lawful king; Gurbani also links rain with blessing, but the rain is sent by God rather than earned by a ruler's justice.
545.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 105, Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
545._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Gurbani makes no causal link between a ruler's justice and rainfall; only the rain-as-blessing image is shared.

546.quote_or_event: “That king sits upon the throne, who is worthy of that throne. Those who realize the True Lord, they alone are the true kings.”
546.explanation: Guru Nanak says rightful kingship rests on worthiness and truth, not on the mere possession of power.
546.tie_back: The Kural says victory comes not from the spear but from the sceptre that does not bend; Guru Nanak likewise locates true kingship in worth and truth rather than in force.
546.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1088, Raag Maaroo (Maaroo ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
546._accuracy_note: Partial: both set righteousness above force, but Guru Nanak speaks of spiritual sovereignty and does not discuss military victory.

547.quote_or_event: “The mythical bull is Dharma, the son of compassion; this is what patiently holds the earth in its place.”
547.explanation: Guru Nanak reinterprets the myth of the bull that bears the earth: what really holds the world in place is dharma, born of compassion.
547.tie_back: The Kural says the king guards the world and justice in turn guards the king; Guru Nanak likewise names righteousness as the power that keeps everything standing.
547.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3, Japji Sahib, Pauri 16, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
547._accuracy_note: Reasonable: dharma as the protector and support of the world fits, but Japji speaks of cosmic order, not a king's administration of justice.

548.quote_or_event: “The Dark Age of Kali Yuga is the knife, and the kings are butchers; righteousness has sprouted wings and flown away.”
548.explanation: Guru Nanak indicts the rulers of his age, who preyed on their subjects instead of giving them justice.
548.tie_back: The Kural says a king who is hard to reach and does not give justice sinks and perishes of himself; Guru Nanak paints that unjust rule, in which righteousness itself has fled.
548.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 145, Raag Maajh (Majh ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
548._accuracy_note: Partial: both condemn rulers who deny justice, but Guru Nanak describes the condition rather than predicting the unjust king's self-destruction or speaking of accessibility.

549.quote_or_event: Guru Hargobind was both pir, spiritual leader, and mir, chieftain of his people, responsible for protecting them against tyranny with force of arms.
549.explanation: From the sixth Guru onward, armed protection of the community became a recognised duty of Sikh leadership.
549.tie_back: The Kural says guarding the people and curbing wrongdoing is no blemish on a king but his proper work; Sikh tradition likewise treats protecting the people against tyranny as a duty, not a stain on spiritual authority.
549.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Sikhism: Guru Hargobind” by W. H. McLeod (paraphrase)
549._accuracy_note: Reasonable: protective force as a duty fits, but Sikh tradition speaks of defence against tyranny rather than a ruler punishing his own subjects' crimes.

550.quote_or_event: “The slanderers are not allowed to stay; they are pulled out by their roots, like useless weeds.”
550.explanation: Guru Arjan says those who malign the Lord's servants cannot stand, but are uprooted like useless weeds.
550.tie_back: The Kural likens punishing the cruel to a farmer pulling weeds to save the young crop; Guru Arjan uses the same weeding image for the removal of wrongdoers.
550.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 683, Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
550._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the weeding image is shared, but the uprooting is God's doing, and Gurbani nowhere endorses a king putting criminals to death.
